[Performance][MRV2] Optimize _penalties_kernel vocab grid to cut scalar overhead (#18613)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

`apply_penalties` launches `_penalties_kernel` on a 2-D grid
`(num_tokens, vocab_grid_size)`, where the second axis was sized as:

```python
vocab_grid_size = min(num_vocab_blocks, 65535 // num_tokens)
```

With Qwen3's vocabulary (151936) and `BLOCK_SIZE = 4096` there are 38
vocab blocks, and `65535 // num_tokens >= 38` for every `num_tokens <=
1724`. The expression therefore evaluates to **38 at every batch size we
actually serve**, i.e. one program per vocab block, and the grid-stride
loop inside the kernel never iterates. Each program pays the per-program
cost once for a single block of work.

That cost is not bandwidth. The kernel is **scalar-bound on A2**:
profiling `glm-5.3-flash-w8a8` with `AiCMetrics.PipeUtilization`, a
representative launch at logits `[8, 154880]` spends 83 % of its
vector-core time in the scalar pipe and 11 % in the vector pipe. Running
a fixed shape in fp32 instead of bf16 moves 1.5× the bytes and costs
**+0.15 %** time, which rules out bandwidth. The scalar unit also
dispatches to every other pipe, so per-program scalar work serialises
everything behind it.

This PR replaces the 2-D grid with a 1-D grid of `get_vectorcore_num()`
programs, each owning a contiguous range of the flattened `(token,
vocab_tile)` work space. The number of programs no longer depends on the
batch size or the vocabulary, and no helper is needed to choose it.

Here is the same launch before and after. `[8, 154880]` means
`num_vocab_blocks = 38`, so the old rule launched 304 programs and the
new one launches 48:

| kernel_details metric | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Duration** | **92.10 µs** | **46.58 µs** | **1.98× faster** |
| `aiv_time` | 80.512 µs | 32.408 µs | 2.48× less |
| `aiv_total_cycles` | 7 149 424 | 2 877 795 | 2.48× less |
| **`aiv_scalar_time`** | **66.788 µs** | **16.168 µs** | **4.13× less**
|
| `aiv_scalar_ratio` | 0.830 | 0.499 | - |
| **`aiv_vec_time`** | **8.834 µs** | **8.128 µs** | **unchanged** |
| `aiv_vec_ratio` | 0.110 | 0.251 | - |
| `aiv_mte2_time` | 4.062 µs | 3.075 µs | 1.32× less |
| `aiv_mte3_time` | 1.235 µs | 1.249 µs | unchanged |
| `aiv_icache_miss_rate` | 0.001 | 0.004 | - |

**The vector time does not move: 8.834 → 8.128 µs.** The same elements
get the same arithmetic whatever the grid is. Every microsecond
recovered came out of the scalar pipe, which is what the change is
designed to do. The kernel goes from 83 % scalar / 11 % vector to 50 %
scalar / 25 % vector, i.e. from overhead-dominated towards
work-dominated.

Over the whole profiled run (18 launches of this operator):

| op_statistic | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Count | 18 | 18 | - |
| **Total time** | **1504.50 µs** | **789.50 µs** | **1.91× less** |
| Avg time | 83.583 µs | 43.861 µs | 1.91× less |
| Min time | 19.98 µs | 19.60 µs | unchanged |
| Max time | 93.34 µs | 54.12 µs | 1.72× less |
| **Share of device time** | **1.715 %** | **0.907 %** | -0.81 pt |

Min time barely moves (19.98 → 19.60 µs), which is expected: those are
the small-batch launches where the old grid was already near-optimal and
there is little per-program cost to amortise. The gain is concentrated
in the larger calls.

**Scope, stated plainly:** this operator was 1.7 % of device time and is
now 0.9 %. It is a sampling-stage kernel, so roughly 1 % of device time
is the entire size of the prize.

### How the work is split

Tiles are numbered flat: tile `t` is token row `t // num_vocab_blocks`,
vocab block `t % num_vocab_blocks`. Program `p` owns `[p·per,
min((p+1)·per, total))` where `per = cdiv(total_tiles, num_workers)`,
converts that range to row bounds once with two integer divisions, and
then nests a row loop over a tile loop. Per-token scalar metadata is
read in the row loop, not the tile loop.

A contiguous range rather than the more obvious grid-stride (`for t in
range(pid, total, num_workers)`) because with 48 workers and 38 blocks
per row the stride is congruent to 2 mod 38, so consecutive iterations
land in different token rows and the per-token scalar reads would be
redone on every tile.

That programs are what cost time can be read off two measured points
without any model. `g` does not change how much vocabulary work there is
- every token row covers all 38 blocks either way - it changes only how
many programs that work is split across:

| `num_tokens` | programs at `g = 38` | µs | programs at `g = 1` | µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 608 | 309.9 | 16 | 275.9 |
| 48 | 1 824 | 555.1 | 48 | 279.9 |
| 128 | 4 864 | 1 182.3 | 128 | 481.5 |
| 192 | 7 296 | 1 673.2 | 192 | 580.7 |

Identical work, 38× the programs, up to 2.9× the time. The old grid is
the one that pays the per-program cost the maximum number of times.

Fitting `time = waves × (P + B × blocks_per_program)` over 118 measured
`(num_tokens, g)` points gives a per-program cost **`P = 7.6 µs`**
against a per-tile cost of **`B = 2.6 µs`** on A2, so a one-block
program, which is what the old grid launched, spent most of its life in
cost that is independent of how many tiles it processes.

**What that per-program cost consists of is not established, and this PR
does not claim to know.** What is measured: it is 95-98 % scalar-pipe
work; it is paid only by programs that enter the vectorised loop body,
since a launch where every program reads the penalty metadata and then
early-returns costs 0.03-0.25 µs per program; `aiv_icache_miss_rate` is
~0.001, which rules out instruction-cache fill; and about 82 % of it
scales with `BLOCK_SIZE` (`P ≈ 1.3 µs + 1.42 ns/element × BLOCK_SIZE`),
so it is not a fixed prologue and it is not the per-token metadata
reads. The change does not depend on the answer: whatever it is made of,
it is paid once per program, so launching fewer programs is faster.

**The split deliberately carries no tuned constant, because the cost it
would encode is platform-specific.** Matched at `k_spec = 3`, the same
fit gives `P = 7.33 µs, B = 3.55 µs` on A2 against `P = 0.104 µs, B =
2.29 µs` on A5: the per-program cost is ~70× lower on A5 while the
per-tile cost moves only 1.55×, so A5 is not scalar-bound and the two
platforms differ in code generation rather than throughput. A variant
that picked a 2-D grid from a cost model fitted on A2 was measured and
is not in this PR: at `num_tokens` 24 and 48 on A5 it chooses a grid
with 1.27× the ideal tile count and lands 14-17 % **slower than main**.
The flat split minimises tiles on the critical path, which is the right
objective under either regime, and it measures at 1.01-1.10× of main on
A5 and never below 1.0.

Measured on the `apply_penalties` call on A2, 48 vector cores,
`vocab_size = 151936` (medians; these include the ~175 µs constant host
launch overhead, which this PR does not address, so the ratios here are
diluted at small batch where the profiler's are not):

| `num_tokens` | main (µs) | this PR (µs) | speedup | speedup, `k_spec =
3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 257.4 | 216.9 | 1.19× | 1.12× |
| 16 | 315.5 | 233.9 | 1.35× | 1.27× |
| 32 | 451.4 | 277.8 | 1.63× | 1.56× |
| 64 | 692.6 | 342.2 | 2.02× | 1.83× |
| 128 | 1188.2 | 478.1 | 2.49× | 2.29× |
| 192 | 1692.8 | 619.8 | 2.73× | 2.64× |
| 256 | 2214.9 | 788.9 | **2.81×** | 2.62× |

On specialization: the kernel keeps `NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS` and `BLOCK_SIZE`
as `tl.constexpr`, since both are fixed per model and shape the loops,
and passes the batch-dependent values (`vocab_size`, `total_tiles`,
`tiles_per_worker`) as runtime arguments. That is one compiled variant
rather than one per batch-size class: sweeping 40 batch sizes produces
no compilation after the first, and a 150-step trace with the batch size
changing every step adds nothing on a second pass. There is no warmup
for this path - `model_executor/warmup/penalties_triton_warmup.py` warms
the v1 sampler in `ops/triton/penalty.py`, not this kernel - so a
variant whose `tl.constexpr` set moves with the batch size would compile
during serving rather than at start-up. A unit test asserts the
constexpr set, so this cannot regress silently.

Net effect on the file: `_vocab_grid_size`, `_FIXED_COST_BLOCKS`,
`_MAX_CORE_DIM` and its assert, and the `functools` import all go, and
the kernel ends up smaller than it is on main.

`BLOCK_SIZE` is promoted to a module-level `VOCAB_BLOCK_SIZE` so tests
can launch the kernel with a matching tile width. On A2, 8192 overflows
UB at compile time, and 1024 and 2048 are measurably slower, so 4096
stays; A5 has more UB available and 8192 compiles there, which is left
for a follow-up since `get_ub_size_bytes()` cannot currently detect it.
`bincount()` keeps its own local `BLOCK_SIZE = 1024`, hence the distinct
name.

`get_vectorcore_num()` is read without calling
`init_device_properties_triton()` first, matching `min_p`, `logprob` and
`bad_words`; the worker initialises device properties at start-up
(`worker.py:489`).

Part of #14157. The issue lists several candidate optimisations; the
measurements above identify the grid as the one that is actually costing
time, so this PR changes only that. The rest are listed at the end.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Output is bit-identical. The kernel's result does not depend on how
the `(token, vocab_tile)` space is partitioned, because every tile is
read, updated and stored by exactly one program with no cross-program
communication and no atomics. That the split is an exact partition is
checked over 2448 combinations of `num_tokens`, `vocab_size`, worker
count and tile width, and the kernel's output is asserted bit-identical
to the current implementation at every benchmarked point and at every
worker count the tests exercise.

### How was this patch tested?

Before this PR the operator tests only parametrised `VOCAB_SIZE =
[1000]`, a single 4096-wide vocab block, so the multi-block path and the
grid-stride loop were never exercised at all. Coverage is added in two
layers, and the two tests that already existed are unchanged.

A CPU unit test, `tests/ut/worker/v2/test_penalties.py` (23 cases),
which needs no NPU and therefore runs on every push via `cpu-ut` without
a label. It replaces `_penalties_kernel` with a fake that records the
launch, and asserts the grid is the core count independent of batch
size, that `total_tiles` and `tiles_per_worker` match the vocabulary
blocking, that `num_tokens == 0` returns without launching, that
replaying the kernel's loops over the split the launcher actually chose
covers every tile exactly once, and that the `tl.constexpr` set is
exactly `{NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS, BLOCK_SIZE}` with the batch-dependent
arguments left at runtime.

Operator correctness on device, in
`tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_penality.py`:

- `test_apply_penalties_multi_vocab_block`: `vocab_size` in `{12800,
151936, 16384}` × `num_tokens` in `{1, 64}` × `num_speculative_tokens`
in `{0, 3}` × `{bf16, fp32}`, against the torch reference. The first two
have a partial tail block and 16384 is an exact multiple of the tile
width, so both mask paths are compared against the reference rather than
only launched.
- `test_apply_penalties_worker_invariance`: launches the kernel directly
at worker counts `{1, 7, num_vocab_blocks, 100}` with and without
speculative decoding, and asserts `torch.equal` between them. One count
per shape of the split: everything on one worker, coprime with the
blocks per row so workers start and end mid-row, exactly row-aligned,
and more workers than tiles. Speculative decoding is included because
`start_idx = token_idx - pos` reaches backwards across token rows, which
is where a mid-row split would corrupt a neighbouring request.
- `test_apply_penalties_penalty_configs`: every penalty combination, at
4 blocks without speculative decoding and again at 38 blocks with it.
One of them is a batch where half the requests have no penalty at all,
which is the case that exercises skipping a row and continuing; the
pre-existing randomised test reaches it only about 7 % of the time per
request.
- **Operator accuracy, before vs after**: on A5 and A3, 480 cases: {1,
5, 64, 256, 2048} tokens × {12800, 16384, 151936} vocab × {0, 3}
speculative tokens × all eight penalty configurations, in BF16 and FP32.
Output is bitwise identical to the pre-optimization kernel in every
case, and all 480 meet the reference accuracy standard against a float32

|golden|`, requiring both ≥99% of elements within tolerance and max
absolute error within the per-dtype limit); 0 failures.

metrics (no overlap between the runs of the two configurations). This
matches what the kernel change predicts for exactly this regime — with
128 requests × 4 token positions per step, the old 2D grid launched one
program per (token, vocab-block) pair, thousands of them, each repeating
the same scalar penalty-parameter loads; the new 1D grid launches one
program per vector core and loads those scalars once per token row, so
the win grows with batch size and is a no-op for small batches.
Speculative-decoding acceptance rate, acceptance length, and
per-position acceptance are unchanged, confirming the optimization does
not alter sampling behaviour.

### Specialization analysis

`apply_penalties` keeps its signature, so callers and the `patch_v2`
override are unaffected. Internally the grid goes from `(rows,
vocab_grid)` to `(vectorcore_num,)`, `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` is gone, and
`total_tiles` / `tiles_per_worker` arrive as runtime ints. Two new entry
conditions: `num_tokens == 0` returns before launching, and the launcher
reads `get_vectorcore_num()`, which needs
`init_device_properties_triton()` (done in `AscendWorker.init_device`).

| Argument | Before | After | Moves with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS`, `BLOCK_SIZE` | constexpr | constexpr | model vocab
/ fixed |
| `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` | constexpr `min(blocks, 65535//rows)` | removed |
batch, above ~1074 rows |
| `total_tiles`, `tiles_per_worker` | — | runtime int | batch |
| `vocab_size`, strides | runtime int | runtime int | model only |

Only tile geometry stays compile-time: every distinct `tl.constexpr`
value compiles its own kernel, so batch-dependent values must stay
runtime. `tests/ut/worker/v2/test_penalties.py` asserts exactly that
set.

Measured with a custom script (Triton's `jit_cache_hook`, split by
phase; GPQA-style waves of 1–128 requests, all three penalties active):
59 distinct row counts collapse to **one specialization class**, with
**0 compiles at startup and 1 on the first penalised request**, nothing
warms this kernel under MRV2, since `kernel_warmup` warms the V1 kernel
in `ops/triton/penalty.py`. Compile count is unchanged from the
baseline: the removed `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` only varied above ~1074 rows,
which 128 requests with 3 MTP draft positions (512 rows) never reaches.

Initial profiling, bottleneck detection, measurements were taken on one
A2 (Ascend910B1, 24 AI cores, 48 vector cores, UB 196608 B) with torch
2.10.0 / torch_npu 2.10.0.post4 / triton-ascend 3.2.0, via
`torch_npu.profiler` with `AiCMetrics.PipeUtilization`. The before/after
profile comes from serving `glm-5.3-flash-w8a8` end to end, with the two
builds differing only in `vllm_ascend/worker/v2/sample/penalties.py`.
The grid sweeps come from a synthetic harness with differential
correctness checking at every point, also run on a 40-core A2 and on A5;
the harness and the raw per-configuration results are available on
request.

+def pack_prompt_bin_mask(
+    prompt_token_ids: list[np.ndarray],

+    """

+    packed = np.ascontiguousarray(packed).view(np.int32)
+    return torch.from_numpy(np.ascontiguousarray(packed)).to(device)

+def unpack_prompt_bin_mask(prompt_bin_mask: torch.Tensor, vocab_size: int) -> torch.Tensor:

+    arr = np.ascontiguousarray(prompt_bin_mask.detach().cpu().numpy())
+    rows = arr.shape[0]
+    bits = np.unpackbits(arr.view(np.uint8).reshape(rows, -1), axis=-1, bitorder="little")
+    bits = np.ascontiguousarray(bits[:, :vocab_size].astype(bool))
+    return torch.from_numpy(bits).to(prompt_bin_mask.device)

+"""Host-side unit tests for the MRV2 penalties launcher.

+These run on CPU. ``_penalties_kernel`` is replaced by a fake that records the
+grid and arguments instead of launching, so what is under test is everything
+``apply_penalties`` decides before the launch -- the grid, the derived tile
+split, the empty-batch guard -- plus the partition arithmetic the kernel
+mirrors and the specialization policy of the kernel signature.
+
+Device numerics (bit-exactness, dtypes, vocabulary tails, speculative decoding)
+are covered by
+``tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_penality.py``,
+which needs an NPU and so cannot live here.

[Feature][Worker] Support Weight Checker on Ascend NPU (#18500)

## Purpose

This PR adds Ascend NPU support for the Weight Checker introduced in
[vLLM PR #51350](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51350) ([RFC
#52689](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52689)).

During RL training, weight updates must reach every rollout worker
correctly. Missing or partially applied updates can cause inconsistent
rollout weights and off-policy training. Weight Checker helps validate
the update path by computing model-parameter checksums, resetting
parameters, and comparing the restored weights against a known baseline.

The upstream vLLM implementation already provides `POST
/weight_checker`, frontend/engine dispatch, and checksum utilities. This
PR integrates the existing functionality into the Ascend NPU worker
without duplicating upstream APIs or engine logic.

## Design

**1. NPU worker integration**

Add the following methods to `NPUWorker` in
`vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py`:

- `compute_weight_checksums()`: compute SHA-256 digests using upstream
`compute_tensor_digests()` and return rank-prefixed parameter names.
- `reset_weights()`: zero model parameters using upstream
`zero_weights()` while leaving buffers unchanged.
- `_weight_checksum_prefix()`: generate unique
`dp{dp}:pp{pp}:pcp{pcp}:tp{tp}:` prefixes using `data_parallel_index`
and PP/PCP/TP rank information.
- `_weight_checksum_model()`: obtain the model from either
`model_runner.get_model()` or `model_runner.model` for compatibility
with different runner interfaces.

The existing `collective_rpc` mechanism dispatches these methods to the
workers. `NPUWorker310` inherits the implementation, although 310P
hardware has not been validated in this PR.

**2. Upstream reuse and version compatibility**

`NPUWorker` directly imports `compute_tensor_digests()` and
`zero_weights()` from vLLM's `weight_checksum` module. The module first
appeared in `v0.31.1rc0`; older versions cannot import `NPUWorker`, even
when Weight Checker is unused.

The current checkout selects vLLM main commit
`24420b7a341af37a9bc3186e6fc6062512e0aa58` and release tag `v0.33.0`.
For PRs targeting main, CPU unit-test CI covers both references; NPU
jobs use the verified main commit by default and also include the
release tag when `main2main` is enabled.

The validation reported below used the verified main commit. It does not
claim a locally completed validation run against `v0.33.0`. This PR adds
no package-level minimum version constraint or runtime guard.

**3. Ascend-specific recovery behavior**

RL configurations automatically disable `weight_nz_mode`, so the
standard RL weight-update path is unaffected. When `weight_nz_mode` is
enabled explicitly, resetting weights emits a warning because the
weight-transfer update path is unavailable in that configuration.
Recovery through `reload_weights()` remains possible where supported.
Users must ensure that a valid recovery path exists before resetting the
parameters.

**4. Tests and documentation**

- Worker unit tests: `tests/ut/worker/test_worker_weight_checker.py`.
- Weight Checker E2E tests:
`tests/e2e/pull_request/two_card/rlhf/state_transitions/test_weight_checker.py`,
with shared helpers under `tests/e2e/common/rlhf/`.
- User documentation: `docs/source/user_guide/feature_guide/rl.md`.

The guide now includes explicit server/trainer device selection, a
trainer example that restores the original checkpoint over HCCL while
keeping generation paused, checks before and after restoration, and
conditional resume after a full checksum match. It also documents
prerequisites and automated validation commands.

With a compatible upstream vLLM and `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`, users can
invoke the existing Weight Checker development endpoint on Ascend NPU:

| Request | Response | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"action": "checksum"}` | `{"checksums": {key: sha256_hex}}` |
Capture the current parameter checksums |
| `{"action": "reset"}` | `{"status": "reset"}` | Zero the covered model
parameters |
| `{"action": "compare", "baseline": {key: sha256_hex}}` | `{"match":
bool, "mismatches": [key]}` | Identify changed or missing parameters |

Recommended verification workflow:

1. Pause inference and capture the checksum baseline.
2. Reset the rollout worker parameters.
3. Restore the **same expected weights** through NPU IPC, HCCL weight
transfer, or `reload_weights()`.
4. Compare against the baseline, verify `match: true`, and resume
inference.

If the trainer has performed a genuine optimization step, the new
weights should not be compared with an old baseline. The baseline must
correspond to the expected weight version.

**Limitations:** As in upstream vLLM, buffers, draft models, and LoRA
adapters are outside the Weight Checker coverage. Quantized/MoE models,
PP/PCP configurations, and 310P hardware were not validated in this
acceptance run. Basic and TP/DP checksum cases use eager mode; IPC/HCCL
transfer cases use the shared RLHF helper's `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`
configuration with capture size 1. Other graph configurations are
outside the claimed automated-test coverage. The development endpoint is
destructive when `reset` is called and should not be exposed to
untrusted clients.

## Test Plan

The test categories follow the [upstream vLLM Weight Checker
PR](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51350): unit tests for
worker/checksum behavior and E2E tests for API behavior, weight
recovery, and distributed-worker coverage. The E2E scenarios live in a
single file whose single-rank lanes use one NPU and whose multi-rank
lanes use two.

**Unit tests (worker integration)**

- Verify that the Weight Checker methods are available on the Ascend
worker classes.
- Verify unique checksum prefixes across dense DP replicas and valid
parameter-name/digest formatting.
- Verify that `reset_weights()` zeros parameters without modifying
buffers.
- Verify that `reset_weights()` warns when `weight_nz_mode` is enabled.
- Verify model lookup with both supported ModelRunner interfaces.
- Run the related HCCL weight-transfer engine tests.

These complement the upstream checksum-utility tests for tensor layouts,
parameter subclasses, and shared parameters; those upstream utility
cases are not reimplemented in vllm-ascend.

**E2E tests (Weight Checker workflow)**

- **API validation:** invalid requests return HTTP 400; `checksum` is
stable; `compare` detects modified and missing baseline keys.
- **Reset and checkpoint recovery:** resetting weights produces
mismatches; `reload_weights()` restores a full match.
- **Weight transfer recovery:** resetting and restoring through real NPU
IPC and HCCL weight transfers produces a full match, including packed
and unpacked transfer modes.
- **Distributed coverage:** TP=2 and DP=2 tests verify that every worker
rank is included in checksums and reset/reload, and that missing-rank
entries are detected.

The NZ-mode warning path is covered by a unit test rather than a
dedicated E2E lane, because RL configurations disable NZ mode
automatically. Upstream route tests are not duplicated because this PR
does not change the frontend routes. The E2E suite requires a paired

+### Weight checker
+
+The Weight Checker helps validate the weight-transfer path during development.
+It computes SHA-256 digests for model parameters on each rank, resets the
+parameters, and checks whether transferring the original weights back restores
+the same digests. See the upstream
+[Weight Checker guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/weight_checker/)
+for the full API.
+
+All three operations use `POST /weight_checker`:
+
+| Action | Purpose | Request body | Response |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `checksum` | Compute the current digest of each checked parameter without changing it. Save the result as the baseline before resetting weights. | `{"action":"checksum"}` | `{"checksums": {key: sha256_hex}}` |
+| `reset` | Zero the checked parameters to test the transfer path. The model cannot serve valid requests until its weights are restored. | `{"action":"reset"}` | `{"status":"reset"}` |
+| `compare` | Compute current digests and compare them with the baseline supplied by the caller. | `{"action":"compare","baseline":{key: sha256_hex}}` | `{"match":bool,"mismatches":[key]}` |
+
+A checksum key has the form `dp{dp}:pp{pp}:pcp{pcp}:tp{tp}:{tensor_name}`,
+so each shard is checked separately. Expert-parallel ranks are identified by
+their DP/PCP/TP coordinates; there is no separate `ep` field. The server does
+not retain the baseline between requests: save the `checksum` response and
+pass its `checksums` object to `compare`.
+
+The standard check transfers the *same original weights* after `reset` and
+expects `compare` to report a full match. An old baseline should not match
+weights changed by a real training step. This procedure validates the
+weight-transfer path, not the correctness of newly trained weights.
+
+#### Example
+
+Use an installed vLLM-Ascend environment with compatible vLLM, CANN and
+TorchNPU, including the compiled Ascend custom operators. The paired vLLM
+must provide the Weight Checker API and the weight-transfer trainer API used
+below. Use the dependency versions selected by your vLLM-Ascend checkout;
+changing only `PYTHONPATH` does not install its custom operators.
+
+This example needs two available NPUs, `curl`, `jq`, and the full
+`Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` checkpoint. The server and trainer must resolve the same
+checkpoint revision. Device IDs 0 and 1 below are examples; replace them
+consistently with two available physical devices. Do not use dummy weights
+or change the model's layer count for this checkpoint round trip.
+
+In terminal 1, start the server on physical NPU 0 and wait until
+`curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health` succeeds:
+
+```bash
+ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1 \
+vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \
+    --weight-transfer-config '{"backend": "hccl"}' \
+    --additional-config '{"rl_config": {"enabled": true}}'
+```
+
+In terminal 2, save the following as `weight_checker_trainer.py`. It uses the
+same trainer API as
+[`rlhf_http_hccl.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/blob/main/examples/rl/rlhf_http_hccl.py),
+but waits for the reset and leaves generation paused after the transfer.
+Do not run that standalone example in the middle of this procedure: it
+requests generation before the transfer and resumes before checksum comparison.
+
+```python
+import torch
+import torch_npu  # noqa: F401
+from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.base import ModuleSource
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.clients import HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.factory import WeightTransferTrainerFactory
+from vllm.utils.network_utils import get_ip, get_open_port
+
+from vllm_ascend.distributed.weight_transfer import register_engine
+from vllm_ascend.distributed.weight_transfer.hccl_engine import HCCLTrainerInitInfo
+
+
+def main():
+    # Both devices are visible here: logical NPU 1 is the trainer's device.
+    torch.accelerator.set_device_index("npu:1")
+    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
+        "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", dtype=torch.bfloat16
+    ).to("npu:1")
+    max_tensor_bytes = max(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in model.parameters())
+    register_engine()
+    engine = WeightTransferTrainerFactory.trainer_init(
+        HCCLTrainerInitInfo(
+            rank=0,
+            master_address=get_ip(),
+            master_port=get_open_port(),
+            world_size=2,  # One trainer and one inference worker.
+            packed=True,
+            packed_buffer_size_bytes=max(max_tensor_bytes + 128 * 2**20, 2**30),
+        ),
+        client=HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000"),
+        source=ModuleSource(model),
+    )
+    try:
+        input(
+            "Trainer ready. Complete pause/checksum/reset in terminal 3, "
+            "then press Enter here to restore the original weights: "
+        )
+        # Owns START -> transfer -> FINISH, including worker RPCs.
+        engine.send_weights()
+        print("Transfer complete. Keep generation paused and compare in terminal 3.")
+    finally:
+        engine.shutdown()
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()
+```
+
+Run it with both devices visible, and wait for the `Trainer ready` prompt
+before resetting the server. Leave this terminal waiting at the prompt:
+
+```bash
+ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 python weight_checker_trainer.py
+```
+
+In terminal 3, pause generation and save the original checksums:
+
+```bash
+URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000
+
+curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/pause?mode=abort"
+curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/weight_checker" \
+    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+    -d '{"action":"checksum"}' > baseline.json
+
+jq -e '.checksums | length > 0' baseline.json
+```
+
+The final command should print `true`. `baseline.json` contains the actual
+parameter names and SHA-256 digests. Its response has this shape (the values
+below are placeholders):
+
+```json
+{
+  "checksums": {
+    "dp0:pp0:pcp0:tp0:<parameter_name>": "<SHA-256 hex digest>"
+  }
+}
+```
+
+Reset the weights while generation remains paused:
+
+```bash
+curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/weight_checker" \
+    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+    -d '{"action":"reset"}'
+```
+
+Expected response:
+
+```json
+{"status":"reset"}
+```
+
+Before restoring the weights, verify that comparison detects the reset.
+Save a reusable comparison request so that the same baseline is used for
+both checks:
+
+```bash
+jq '{action: "compare", baseline: .checksums}' baseline.json > compare-request.json
+curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/weight_checker" \
+    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+    --data-binary @compare-request.json > after-reset.json
+jq -e '.match == false and (.mismatches | length > 0)' after-reset.json
+```
+
+The final command should print `true`. Now press Enter in terminal 2 to
+transfer the *original checkpoint weights*, and wait for `Transfer complete`
+and a successful trainer exit. This step must not perform a training update
+or resume generation.
+
+Back in terminal 3, compare the restored weights with the saved baseline:
+
+```bash
+curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/weight_checker" \
+    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+    --data-binary @compare-request.json > after-restore.json
+cat after-restore.json
+```
+
+Expected response after a successful restore:
+
+```json
+{"match":true,"mismatches":[]}
+```
+
+If `match` is `false`, inspect `mismatches` and restore the weights before
+serving requests. Resume generation only after a full match:
+
+```bash
+jq -e '.match == true and (.mismatches | length == 0)' after-restore.json && \
+    curl -fsS -X POST "$URL/resume"
+```
+
+Finally, verify that generation works again:
+
+```bash
+curl -fsS "$URL/v1/completions" \
+    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+    -d '{"model":"Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B","prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":16,"temperature":0}'
+```
+
+#### Automated checks
+
+Run these commands from the repository root in the installed environment:
+
+```bash
+bash format.sh ci
+python -m pytest -q \
+    tests/ut/worker/test_worker_weight_checker.py \
+    tests/ut/distributed/weight_transfer/test_hccl_engine.py
+ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 VLLM_RL_TEST_DEVICE_INDEX=0 \
+python -m pytest -sv -ra \
+    tests/e2e/pull_request/two_card/rlhf/state_transitions/test_weight_checker.py
+```
+
+The unit tests cover worker integration and mocked HCCL behavior. The E2E
+suite needs two NPUs and the full `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` checkpoint. It covers
+checksum/reset/reload, packed and unpacked IPC/HCCL transfers, and TP=2/DP=2
+rank coverage. Its shared helpers live under `tests/e2e/common/rlhf/`.
+`VLLM_RL_TEST_DEVICE_INDEX` is a logical index into the visible device list;
+the trainer uses the next device. Check the pytest summary for skipped cases
+before claiming the full suite passed.
+
+Basic and TP/DP checksum cases use eager mode. Transfer cases use the shared
+RLHF helper's `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` configuration with capture size 1. Other
+graph configurations require separate validation.
+
+#### Operational constraints
+
+- Stay paused from `checksum` through `compare`. Weights are invalid between
+  `reset` and the transfer, and EPLB may move experts while serving. The
+  worker methods do not enforce the pause; the caller must do so.
+- Before `reset`, confirm that a recovery path is available: a working
+  weight-transfer configuration or a checkpoint that `reload_weights` can
+  restore. In RL mode, `rl_config.enabled=true` disables FRACTAL_NZ by setting
+  `weight_nz_mode=0`. In a non-RL deployment where `weight_nz_mode` remains
+  enabled, the weight-update transaction cannot start; checkpoint reload may
+  be needed to recover after `reset`.
+- If the transfer or comparison fails, keep generation paused and restore the
+  weights before resuming. The engine must be awake: sleep levels 1 and 2
+  release weight memory.
+- `reset` is a destructive development operation. Keep development endpoints
+  within a trusted access boundary and do not expose them to the public
+  internet.
+
+#### Limitations
+
+In addition to the
+[upstream limitations](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/weight_checker/#limitations):
+
+- Weights held as buffers rather than parameters, such as some quantization
+  repacking paths, are invisible to the checker.
+- MoE weights padded beyond the checkpoint shape may report false mismatches;
+  validate the behavior with the target model before relying on `compare`.
+- Ascend 310P has not yet been verified with the Weight Checker.
+

+"""Weight Checker end-to-end tests on Ascend NPU.
+
+Single-card scenarios run on the inference device alone; multi-rank
+scenarios use the inference and trainer devices together. This file lives
+in the two_card lane so the CI runner always provides both cards. Covered:
+request validation, digest stability, key coverage, the reset ->
+checkpoint-reload recovery, the NPU IPC transfer round trip, TP2/DP2 rank
+coverage with missing-rank detection, and the cross-NPU HCCL round trip.
+
+The Weight Checker exposes three dev-mode actions over
+POST /weight_checker — checksum, reset and compare — so an RL stack can
+prove that a weight update landed on every rank. The fixed-random weight
+source and transfer setup are shared with the NPU weight-transfer tests in
+tests/e2e/common/rlhf/weight_transfer/.
+"""
+
+import json
+import os
+from typing import Any
+
+import pytest
+import requests
+import torch
+import torch_npu  # noqa: F401  # registers the NPU backend
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.clients import HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.factory import WeightTransferTrainerFactory
+from vllm.utils.network_utils import get_ip, get_open_port
+
+from tests.e2e.common.rlhf.common import (
+    CONTROL_TIMEOUT,
+    register_engines_once,
+    server_visible_devices,
+    wait_for_free_device_memory,
+)
+from tests.e2e.common.rlhf.common import (
+    post_control as post_route,
+)
+from tests.e2e.common.rlhf.weight_transfer.case import WeightUpdateModelCase
+from tests.e2e.common.rlhf.weight_transfer.reference_check import live_update_serve_args
+from tests.e2e.common.rlhf.weight_transfer.weight_source import (
+    FixedRandomWeightSource,
+    packed_buffer_size_for,
+)
+from tests.e2e.conftest import RemoteOpenAIServer
+
+RELOAD_TIMEOUT = 300
+
+
+def weight_checker(server, action: str, baseline: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> requests.Response:
+    """Call POST /weight_checker; compare also needs a baseline."""
+    body: dict[str, Any] = {"action": action}
+    if baseline is not None:
+        body["baseline"] = baseline
+    return requests.post(server.url_for("weight_checker"), json=body, timeout=RELOAD_TIMEOUT)
+
+
+def checksums(server) -> dict[str, str]:
+    """Return the server's per-parameter weight checksums."""
+    response = weight_checker(server, "checksum")
+    response.raise_for_status()
+    return response.json()["checksums"]
+
+
+def ranks(keys) -> set[str]:
+    """Extract dp:pp:pcp:tp rank prefixes from checksum keys."""
+    return {key.rsplit(":", 1)[0] for key in keys}
+
+
+# Matches the validated acceptance setup; leaves HBM headroom for the
+# co-located trainer in the same-chip transfer lanes.
+GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION = 0.25
+MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"
+HF_OVERRIDES: dict[str, Any] = {}
+# Physical cards; see the NPU weight-transfer tests.
+INFERENCE_DEVICE_INDEX = int(os.environ.get("VLLM_RL_TEST_DEVICE_INDEX", "0"))
+TRAINER_DEVICE_INDEX = INFERENCE_DEVICE_INDEX + 1
+
+CHECKER_CASE = WeightUpdateModelCase(
+    id="qwen3-0.6b-checker",
+    model=MODEL,
+    hf_overrides=HF_OVERRIDES,
+)
+

+    torch.npu.device_count() < 1,
+    reason="Single-card Weight Checker scenarios require at least 1 NPU.",
+)
+requires_two_npus = pytest.mark.skipif(
+    torch.npu.device_count() < 2,
+    reason="Multi-rank Weight Checker scenarios require at least 2 NPUs.",
+)
+
+
+def _basic_serve_args(port: int, *, extra_args=()) -> list[str]:
+    return [
+        "--dtype",
+        "bfloat16",
+        "--max-model-len",
+        "1024",
+        "--gpu-memory-utilization",
+        str(GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION),
+        "--distributed-executor-backend",
+        "mp",
+        "--hf-overrides",
+        json.dumps(HF_OVERRIDES),
+        "--additional-config",
+        json.dumps({"weight_nz_mode": 0}),
+        "--port",
+        str(port),
+        "--enforce-eager",
+        *extra_args,

+
+
+def _env_dict(*device_indexes: int) -> dict[str, str]:

+        "ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES": server_visible_devices(device_indexes[0], len(device_indexes)),

+@pytest.fixture(scope="module")

+@requires_one_npu

+    response = weight_checker(checker_server, "compare", altered)

+    names = {key.split(":", 4)[-1] for key in baseline}
+    assert all("." in name for name in names)

[Doc][Misc] Improve MiniMax, Qwen3 and Step-5 deployment tutorials (#21170)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

Improve five model deployment tutorials so users can prepare the
environment, select the correct weights and service endpoints, and
understand verification and evaluation results.

- **MiniMax-M3.1-Flash:** explain Ascend-adapted weight sources and path
placeholders; add container/NPU checks and source installation steps;
make the A3 Decode graph-capture limit explicit; correct the AISBench
endpoint and describe expected performance metrics.
- **MiniMax-M3:** organize thinking/parser settings under deployment and
complete the functional, accuracy, and performance chapter layout. Add
source installation and service verification guidance, clarify weight
sources, and update PD proxy listener examples to `0.0.0.0` while
retaining the real Prefill backend addresses.
- **Qwen3-30B-A3B:** clarify weight sources, path placeholders, served
model names, and verification steps; standardize the GSM8K performance
example and explain its output.
- **Qwen3-Dense:** add official BF16 download sources, clarify local
paths versus ModelScope repository paths, expand key parameter and
service-check guidance, and correct the performance-evaluation
description.
- **Step-5-Preview:** document the experimental runtime and container
checks, clarify multi-node DP/TP and request endpoints, and add AISBench
performance instructions, tuning guidance, and an FAQ while retaining
the existing serving scripts and accuracy results.
- Fix Markdown block spacing and blockquote formatting, the MiniMax-M3
scheduler-argument URL fragment, and the Step-5 declaration link.

Existing reported accuracy values are retained. New evaluation
instructions describe example workloads and expected metrics, not newly
measured performance results.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No runtime, API, or default behavior changes. This PR updates
documentation and example configurations only. No release note fragment
is required.

### How was this patch tested?

- `git diff --check` passed.
- Markdown lint passed for all five changed documents using
`markdownlint-cli 0.45.0` and the repository's `.markdownlint.yaml`.
- Checked Markdown rendering, local file references, and heading
anchors, including included installation content. Corrected the broken
Step-5 declaration link.
- Checked 54 unique external link destinations; all pages were
reachable, including one confirmed through an independent browser fetch
after a local TLS failure. Corrected and rechecked the MiniMax-M3
scheduler-argument anchor.
- Parsed the added Python evaluation examples and checked added shell
examples with `bash -n`. Verified that the original Step-5 serving
scripts and accuracy rows are unchanged.
- `bash format.sh ci` could not complete because `pre-commit` is not
installed locally. A full documentation-site build was not run.
- No model services, NPU accuracy evaluations, or performance benchmarks
were run for this update. No runtime tests were added for these
documentation changes.

---

### Checklist

#### Testing

The runtime-specific checklist items below are not applicable to this
documentation-only change.

- [ ] **Boundary / edge-case coverage**: I reviewed whether this change
involves
boundary conditions (e.g. empty input, single/zero element, min/max
values,
off-by-one, sequence-length limits, integer overflow). Where applicable,
I
added unit tests covering these edge cases in `tests/ut/` or
`tests/e2e/`.
- [ ] **Regression test**: If this PR fixes a bug, I added a regression
test
  that would fail without the fix.
- [ ] **Error / failure path coverage**: I covered abnormal paths
(exceptions,
timeouts, out-of-range, division by zero) in addition to the happy path.
- [ ] **Meaningful & reliable tests**: New tests assert real behavior
and are
  not written merely to satisfy CI.
- [ ] **Performance impact**: If this PR touches a performance-sensitive
path,
  I attached benchmark results and added performance regression tests.

+## 9 Performance Tuning
+
+### 9.1 Recommended Configurations
+
+Use the commands in [Section 5](#5-online-service-deployment) as starting configurations. They are not globally optimal: the appropriate settings depend on request lengths, concurrency, and the available device memory. Evaluate each adjustment with the same workload and compare latency, throughput, and memory use. This preview does not provide validated single-node or PD-disaggregated alternatives.
+
+| Scenario | Starting Configuration | Validation |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Long context | Multi-node co-located example in Section 5.1 with `max-model-len=1048576`; ensure prompt and generated tokens fit together. | KV-cache capacity and failed requests at the intended concurrency. |
+| Low latency | The same deployment with reduced offered request concurrency. | TTFT and TPOT under the target input/output lengths. |
+| High throughput | The same deployment with a gradually increased request rate. | Successful request/output-token throughput, latency, and memory use. |
+
+### 9.2 Tuning Guidelines
+

+## 10 FAQ

commits.message: [Feature][MRV2] Support LM head TP with probabilistic draft sampling (#21209) ### What this PR does / why we need it? Enable LM head TP together with `draft_sample_method="probabilistic"` in Model Runner V2. Previously, the shared draft wrapper padded hidden states before calling upstream `sample_draft` and only trimmed the sampled token IDs afterward. Probabilistic sampling would therefore consume extra logits rows without corresponding request metadata, risking invalid mapping reads and draft-logits cache writes; the combination was rejected. Move alignment into `LmheadTPDraftSamplingMixin.compute_draft_logits`: pad hidden states for the LM-head collectives, then trim logits back to the original input row count **before** upstream sampling. This preserves original graph-padding rows and DFlash's multiple rows per request while keeping LM-head-only padding out of the sampler. - Enable probabilistic sampling for MTP, Eagle, Gemma4 MTP and DFlash through the shared hook. - Allow DSpark through initialization validation; its existing model-level pad/trim path already trims before its independent sampling flow and remains unchanged. - Preserve rejection of DFlash2/LiLiCorr and the local-argmax/adaptive-verification restrictions. Standalone AR and multi-module MTP do not inherit this hook. - Keep upstream vLLM code and sampling kernels unchanged. ### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change? Yes. Users can combine LM head TP with probabilistic draft sampling for the supported algorithms above. The existing greedy sampling path remains covered. Release note: `release_notes/fragments/21209.yaml`. ### How was this patch tested? #### CPU unit tests ```bash python -m pytest -q \ tests/ut/worker/v2/test_lmhead_tp_utils.py \ tests/ut/worker/test_model_runner_v2_finegrained_tp.py \ tests/ut/spec_decode/test_dspark_speculator.py \ tests/ut/spec_decode/test_gemma4_speculator_v2.py \ tests/ut/patch/worker/test_patch_v2_gumbel.py ``` **122 passed**, including 45 new cases. Coverage includes feature ON/OFF, greedy/probabilistic dispatch, pre-sampling row trimming, original graph padding, DFlash multi-row metadata, cache destinations, empty/full/over-capacity inputs, module-index forwarding and algorithm support boundaries. The real upstream `sample_draft` and Ascend logits hook run with CPU tensors; LM-head computation and the low-level sampler are test doubles, so these UTs do not claim to validate the device sampling kernel. An isolated mutation check removed the crop only in the test process: all 12 feature-ON sampling cases failed as expected, while all 12 feature-OFF cases passed. Ruff lint, Ruff format checks on all five changed Python files, and `git diff --check` passed. Full `bash format.sh ci` was attempted but could not initialize the actionlint pre-commit dependency because the configured proxy refused the connection; full pre-commit/CI verification remains outstanding. #### Ascend NPU accuracy and acceptance validation Ran GLM-5.2-W4A8 with both MTP and DSpark on Ascend 910 hardware, using AISBench and the same complete GSM8K test set (1,319 questions per run). For each algorithm, compared the fixed code with LM head TP ON and OFF; the paired runs used identical model, source, dataset, client configuration and other server settings. - TP=8, DP=2; LM head TP=2 (ON) versus default 1 (OFF). - `draft_sample_method="probabilistic"`, request temperature=0.7, seed=1024, concurrency=32, maximum output=8192 tokens. - MTP: 3 draft tokens, model-provided weights. DSpark: 7 draft tokens, GLM-5.2-speculator.dspark weights. - Server settings follow `tests/e2e/cases/models/configs/GLM/GLM-5.2-W4A8-MTP-A3-V2.yaml` and `GLM-5.2-W4A8-DSpark-A3-V2.yaml`, with the overrides above. Decoder configuration used `enforce_eager=true`; target graph mode was `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`. - Upstream vLLM: `24420b7a341af37a9bc3186e6fc6062512e0aa58`; Ascend base: `9649d5a76209159b773a46275c95ea743e44beb7` plus this production patch. - All four runs completed 1,319 successful predictions. Audited per-question scoring, paired dataset/configuration/source hashes and Prometheus counter deltas from both DP engines. | Algorithm | LM head TP | Correct | GSM8K accuracy | Mean accepted draft tokens / round | Accepted / proposed draft tokens | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | MTP | 1 (OFF) | 1277/1319 | 96.8158% | 2.2898 | 76.3281% | | MTP | 2 (ON) | 1274/1319 | 96.5883% | 2.3009 | 76.6980% | | DSPARK | 1 (OFF) | 1278/1319 | 96.8916% | 3.8457 | 54.9383% | | DSPARK | 2 (ON) | 1273/1319 | 96.5125% | 3.8679 | 55.2551% | Per-position acceptance below is the accepted-token count at that position divided by the total draft rounds, aggregated over both DP engines (not conditional acceptance given the preceding position). | Algorithm | Draft position | LM head TP OFF | LM head TP ON | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | MTP | 1 | 91.0504% | 91.2728% | | MTP | 2 | 76.6894% | 77.0546% | | MTP | 3 | 61.2447% | 61.7665% | | DSPARK | 1 | 89.2328% | 89.4314% | | DSPARK | 2 | 75.1313% | 75.4195% | | DSPARK | 3 | 62.4319% | 62.8388% | | DSPARK | 4 | 51.7117% | 52.0824% | | DSPARK | 5 | 42.7283% | 43.0250% | | DSPARK | 6 | 34.9984% | 35.3003% | | DSPARK | 7 | 28.3336% | 28.6882% | Accuracy and acceptance behaved normally in these runs, with no obvious degradation observed when enabling LM head TP. ON/OFF accuracy differed by 3 questions for MTP and 5 for DSpark; mean acceptance was slightly higher with LM head TP ON. These single stochastic runs do not establish distributional equivalence. MTP and DSpark use different draft lengths, so their accepted/proposed ratios should not be interpreted as a direct performance ranking. The temperature-0 YAML reference values were not used as an equivalent-condition baseline. No dedicated throughput/latency performance regression benchmark was added; this PR reports correctness and acceptance validation. --- ### Checklist #### Testing - [x] **Boundary / edge-case coverage**: empty inputs, capacity limits, overflow, graph padding and multi-row draft inputs. - [x] **Regression test**: removing pre-sampling trimming fails the feature-ON cases. - [x] **Error / failure path coverage**: over-capacity inputs and unsupported combinations. - [x] **Meaningful & reliable tests**: assertions cover production hook behavior, sampler arguments and cache destinations. - [ ] **Performance impact**: accuracy and acceptance results are provided; dedicated performance benchmarks/regression tests remain unrun. - vLLM main: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/24420b7a341af37a9bc3186e6fc6062512e0aa58 --------- Signed-off-by: shenyunyang <15713002151@163.com>

[Test] Fix missing QuantType in Kimi SiTU quantization fixture (#21504)

### What this PR does / why we need it?
Add `QuantType` to the Kimi SiTU quantization test fixture's execution
scope.

#18053 added a class attribute referencing `QuantType`. The test loads
the class through AST without its module imports, causing all 20 cases
to fail with `NameError`.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
N/A

### How was this patch tested?
by ci

---

### Checklist

#### Testing

- [x] **Boundary / edge-case coverage**: I reviewed whether this change
involves
boundary conditions (e.g. empty input, single/zero element, min/max
values,
off-by-one, sequence-length limits, integer overflow). Where applicable,
I
added unit tests covering these edge cases in `tests/ut/` or
`tests/e2e/`.
- [x] **Regression test**: If this PR fixes a bug, I added a regression
test
  that would fail without the fix.
- [x] **Error / failure path coverage**: I covered abnormal paths
(exceptions,
timeouts, out-of-range, division by zero) in addition to the happy path.
- [x] **Meaningful & reliable tests**: New tests assert real behavior
and are
  not written merely to satisfy CI.
- [x] **Performance impact**: If this PR touches a performance-sensitive
path,
  I attached benchmark results and added performance regression tests.
